metadata.title: What key contextual factors contribute to students’ reading literacy among top-performing countries and economies? Statistical and machine learning analyses

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for reading literacy and constructs an analytic sample consisting of students from B-S-J-Z (Beijing-Shanghai-Jiangsu-Zhejiang), Singapore, and Macau, plus a comparison analysis using all 79 PISA 2018 participating countries/economies. The manuscript reports using PV1READ as the outcome and describes missing-value imputation (median imputation) and exclusion of students with reading scores below 262, but it does not report whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied. Because the paper does not mention any PISA weight variables (e.g., student design weights) or replicate-weight procedures, weighting cannot be confirmed; the most transparent interpretation is that the analysis may be unweighted or weight handling is omitted from reporting. The data preparation also includes selecting the specified student-level contextual factors (background, reading metacognitive strategies, and motivation/attitudes) and then splitting the data into 80% training and 20% testing for the GBDT model.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 student-level data. The analytic sample for the main country/economy-focused analyses includes 12,058 B-S-J-Z students, 6,676 Singapore students, and 3,775 Macau students. For missing values, the study imputes missing values using the median of each factor. Students with reading literacy scores below 262 are excluded because PISA 2018 did not specify reading literacy levels for scores below 262. For the machine learning model, the dataset is further split into 80% training and 20% testing; hyperparameters are tuned via grid search with 10-fold cross-validation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (PV1READ) — B-S-J-Z, Singapore, and Macau (student-level)
main_findings.performance_metrics: GBDT (GBDT with tuned hyperparameters): R² = 0.499; RMSE = 68.34 (for B-S-J-Z, Singapore and Macau combined). Shapley value decomposition (R² contribution rates): metacognitive strategies 53.83% (assessing credibility 42.46%, summarizing information 21.33%, understanding and remembering 19.51%), ESCS 37.39 (coefficient), student background 18.87%, reading motivation/attitudes 27.30%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data (PV1READ) for B-S-J-Z, Singapore, and Macau students, the study leveraged assessing credibility, summarizing information, ESCS, reading interest, and understanding and remembering to predict reading literacy, finding that metacognitive strategies—especially assessing credibility—dominated both Shapley contribution rates and GBDT relative importance. This indicates that reading-improvement policies in high-performing contexts should prioritize metacognitive instruction (e.g., credibility evaluation and summarization) alongside socioeconomic-support measures, while noting that the analysis is cross-sectional and uses PV1READ as a single plausible value.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 reading literacy at the student level, focusing on three top-performing Asian economies/economy groupings: B-S-J-Z (China), Singapore, and Macau, and also reports comparisons using all 79 PISA 2018 participating countries/economies. The dependent variable is PV1READ (the first plausible value for reading), and missing values are imputed using the median of each factor; students with reading scores below 262 are excluded. The authors first use Shapley value decomposition to quantify how categories of contextual factors contribute to variance in reading literacy, then train a gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT) model to predict reading scores using the identified factors. For the combined top-performing group, the final GBDT model achieves R² = 0.499 with RMSE = 68.34, and assessing credibility is the highest-importance predictor (relative importance ~38%). The paper does not report survey-weight usage, and the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation of the predictive associations.
